general.sanskritUnreviewed: Sanskrit is a work in progress: the names shown were written for this app and haven't been checked by a Sanskrit reader, and anything the astrology engine itself translates currently falls back to Hindi.
general.signLabelHint: How each house names its rasi: the number (1 = Aries … 12 = Pisces, as in a traditional chart), the glyph (♈︎), coloured by element — fire, earth, air, water — both, or the short name (Ar). Hover a house to see the sign's full name whichever you pick.
general.praveshaBasisHint: Which pravesha ladder the Daily and Monthly readings are cast on. Solar = the Tajaka ladder (Maasa Pravesha, a solar month). Lunar = the tithi ladder (the birth-tithi return, a lunar month). Only the Monthly page can override it — there the basis picks the window itself, a solar month or a lunar one. The Fortnight is always lunar (there is no solar fortnight). Varshaphal is always solar and Tithi Pravesha always lunar, so this setting does not touch them.
general.themeHint: System follows your device's light/dark setting, and changes with it. Light and Dark stay put.
general.densityHint: Compact fits more on screen; Comfortable gives cards and tiles more room. Applies everywhere, straight away.
general.startupProfileHint: Whether signing in goes straight to a chart or to the profile picker. Opening your last profile falls back to your default profile, and to the picker if you have several profiles and no default.
general.pageHintsHint: A one-line “What am I looking at?” on your first visit to each page. Auto shows them for your first two weeks; On brings back any you dismissed.

privacy.title: What hosted AI models may see
privacy.intro: Readings are written from a chart this app has already calculated, so the AI doesn't need your birth date, time or place. By default they are held back from hosted models (Gemini, OpenAI, OpenRouter) — the date is replaced by your age. Tick an item to send it anyway.

privacy.local: You're using a self-hosted model on this machine or your network, so it is sent everything — these switches only apply when a reading goes to a hosted provider (including as a fallback when the local model is busy).
privacy.hosted: These switches apply to every reading, chat and digest sent to the provider you've chosen.
privacy.alwaysSent: Always sent, to any model: the calculated chart (planets, houses, dashas, transits), the profile's name, and what you write — your questions and, when the AI looks them up, your journal entries.
privacy.geminiFree: Gemini's free tier may use prompts to improve Google's products. Use a paid Gemini key, or a different provider, if that matters to you.

rectify.title: Birth-Time Rectification

methodDesc.nakshatra: Checks the Moon's birth star against the star expected from the exact birth moment, and nudges the time (±30 min) so they agree. Needs no extra input.
methodDesc.lagna: Checks the rising sign (Lagna) against the Moon and Maandi in the Rasi and Navamsa, nudging the time so the Lagna sits in a supportive relationship.
methodDesc.janma: Checks the classical birth-time gender indication and nudges the time so it agrees with the stated gender. Requires selecting a gender.

bhrigu.title: Bhrigu / Nadi Markers
bhrigu.subtitle: Yearly life markers (traditional predictive aid)

nadi.title: Nadi Karakas
nadi.subtitle: Karaka significators & event timing (traditional predictive aid)
nadi.intro: The Nadi karaka method reads the chart through the planets' fixed natural significators and their placement by sign — setting houses and aspects aside. Conjunctions (planets sharing a sign) carry the weight, and a slow graha transiting a karaka's sign is what times its events.
nadi.karakasIntro: Each graha is the natural significator of certain affairs. Read it through the sign it sits in (and that sign's lord), its star-lord, and whom it joins.
nadi.themesIntro: Each life area, headed by its karaka — so you can see at a glance where marriage, career or children are anchored.
nadi.triggersIntro: The next ingress of the slow movers — Jupiter, Saturn and Rahu — into the pivotal karaka signs. A slow graha reaching a karaka's sign is treated as a turning point.
nadi.noTriggers: No trigger found in the searched horizon.
nadi.aiHint: Get a plain-language reading of the karakas and their timing.
nadi.disclaimer: These are indicative karaka signals, a traditional predictive aid — not a fated forecast. Free will shapes the outcome.

strength.title: Planetary Strength

strength.compositionIntro: The six sources that make up each planet's Shadbala, shown as a share of its total.
strength.bhavaIntro: How well-founded each of the twelve houses is, in the order 1–12.
strength.vimsopakaIntro: How consistently each planet holds good dignity across the sixteen divisional charts (out of 20).

strength.aiHint: Get a plain-language reading of the strengths and what needs support.
strength.disclaimer: Strength shows capacity to deliver, not whether results are favourable — read it with the rest of the chart.
strength.compositionTable: The figures behind the bars. The six components are in virupas; the total and the required minimum are in rupas (60 virupas = 1 rupa).

sadeSati.title: Sade Sati
sadeSati.subtitle: Saturn's transits over your Moon
sadeSati.intro: Sade Sati is the ~7½-year period when Saturn transits the 12th, 1st and 2nd signs from your natal Moon. A time of maturing and consolidation — traditionally testing, but a chapter of growth, not doom. It comes to everyone: Saturn circles the zodiac about every 29½ years, so most people pass through it two or three times — roughly a quarter of a lifetime.

sadeSati.aiHint: Get a calm, plain-language reading of your Sade Sati and Saturn periods.
sadeSati.disclaimer: Sade Sati is a period of growth and maturing, not a curse — this is indicative guidance, not a prediction of misfortune.

a.aiAccurate: It faithfully reports what the calculations say and interprets them in the tradition's own terms — the maths is real astronomy. Whether astrology itself predicts anything is a question this app can't settle for you. Please treat every reading as reflection, not instruction, and never as medical, legal or financial advice. AI models can also simply be wrong, and this one occasionally will be.
a.aiCorrectionNote: Every reading is checked against your own chart before you see it. The app pulls out the factual statements — which house a planet sits in, which sign, which nakshatra, who rules a house, whether a planet is retrograde or combust — and compares each one with what was actually calculated for your birth details. If the AI has contradicted the chart, the app asks it again, naming the mistake; most of the time the second answer is right and you never see any of this. When something still doesn't match, that box appears and tells you what the chart really says. The interpretation around it may still be worth reading — but where the words and the chart disagree, the chart is right, and the note is there so you aren't left to spot it yourself.
a.aiHistory: Everything is saved automatically. AI History (in My Notebook, next to your Astro-Journal) holds every reading and chat, and you can reopen any of them exactly as they were. Readings also show up under the page that produced them.
a.aiLongWait: Yes. A local model can take several minutes on a long question, and the answer is written on the server, not in your browser — so you can switch pages, lock your phone or close the tab. While it's working, the ✦ pill in the top bar shows it (and History lists it under "In progress"). When it's done the pill says it's ready: tap it to open the answer on its own page. It's also saved to History like any other reading.
a.aiModes: Full context hands the model your whole chart up front — thorough, and better for open-ended questions, but slower and heavier. Smart lookup gives it a summary plus the ability to fetch specific calculations on demand, which is quicker and usually enough. If an answer seems to have missed something, switch to Full context and ask again.
a.aiWhatIsIt: A conversational astrologer that has already been handed your chart. You can ask it anything — "what does my chart say about money?", "explain my current period", "what is a nakshatra?" — and ask follow-ups. It's also the layer that writes the readings on other pages.
a.aiWhatItSees: The chart data for the profile you have selected: planetary positions, houses, periods, yogas and whatever the specific page computed, plus the profile's name and what you type. A local model also sees the birth date, time and place; a cloud provider doesn't, unless you allow it in Settings → AI (see "What do cloud AI providers get sent?" under Privacy). It never sees your password, your email or other users' data.
a.privAiProviders: Everything a reading needs, and no more by default. The app calculates the chart itself, so a cloud provider (Gemini, OpenAI, OpenRouter) is sent the calculated chart — planets, houses, periods, transits — plus the profile's name, your questions, and any journal entries the AI looks up for you. Your birth date, time and place are held back: the date is replaced by your age. You can choose to send any of them in Settings → AI. A model you run yourself (Ollama on your computer or home network) is always sent everything, since nothing leaves. Note that the free Gemini tier may use prompts to improve Google's products; a paid key doesn't.
a.aiWhichModel: Whichever you've configured in Settings → AI. You can point it at a local model running on your own machine (nothing leaves home) or at a cloud provider with your own API key. The model's name is shown on each reading, so you can always tell what wrote it.
a.aiUnavailable: A local model shares its graphics card with everything else on that machine, so if something heavier is running the model may have nowhere to load itself. When that happens the app says so instead of inventing an answer, and it tries whatever else it can reach — a cloud provider you've added a key for, or a slower CPU-only endpoint if one is configured. Settings → System shows the local model as "Busy" while this lasts, with a rough countdown. Scheduled digests hold back for up to an hour and a half rather than arriving thinner than usual, and go out with their highlights after that. Just ask again in a few minutes; nothing is broken and nothing was lost.
a.believe: Not at all. Plenty of people read a chart the way they'd read a personality sketch or a journalling prompt: something to think with, not something to obey. The app is deliberately written to describe tendencies rather than issue verdicts, and nothing here should replace medical, legal or financial advice.
a.essentialsVsEverything: No. The app starts in Essentials, which shows about a dozen pages most people want. Everything unlocks the full set — over thirty — including the specialist systems. Switch any time in Settings → General → View mode. Nothing is ever taken away from you; Essentials just doesn't advertise it all at once.
a.tryWithoutAccount: Yes. On the front page, enter your date, time and place of birth under “See your chart in plain words” and you'll get your Rising sign, Moon sign, birth star and the chapter of life you're in now — no account needed. Nothing is saved on our side: the details stay in that browser tab. If you then create an account, they're carried straight into your first profile so you don't type them twice. Asking the AI astrologer needs an account, because every question costs real computing time.
a.firstWeek: Help for your first couple of weeks. The checklist on the dashboard suggests four things worth doing once — see your chart explained, ask a first question, turn on the daily digest, take the short quiz on your own chart — and ticks each off when you actually do it; hide it any time with the ×. The one-line note at the top of a page says what that page is for, the first time you open it. Both follow you across devices. Settings → General → Page hints turns the notes on or off for good; “On” also brings back any you dismissed.
a.featAdvanced: One long page of the classical measurements that sit behind a reading. Ashtakavarga scores every sign by bindus (points) from each planet, and the combined Sarvashtakavarga shows which signs are strong for you. The arudha padas show how each house's affairs appear to the world. You'll also find a longevity (ayu) indication, planetary conditions such as combust or retrograde, the avasthas (the "state" each planet is in, like infant or old, awake or asleep), and a friendship table showing which planets treat each other as friend, neutral or enemy. A few things that used to be repeated here now live in one place each, and the page links to them: Shadbala on Planetary Strength, the chara karakas on Jaimini, the special lagnas and upagrahas on Sensitive Points, and the aspects on the Birth Chart. For the curious; nothing here is needed for normal use.
a.featAlmanac: The traditional calendar: the day's panchanga, auspicious and inauspicious windows, festivals and vratha dates, and eclipses. Each day also shows sunrise and sunset, Rahu Kalam and the other daily windows, and the Islamic (Hijri) date.
a.featBhava: The houses again, but drawn by their actual cusps rather than by whole signs. House systems (Sripati, Placidus, KP, Equal) disagree about where a house begins, and this lets you see the effect.
a.featBhrigu: The Bhrigu Bindu — a calculated midpoint between the Moon and Rahu — and related sensitive points, used by some readers to time events.
a.featNadi: The Nadi karaka method reads the chart through the planets' fixed natural significators and their placement by sign — setting houses and aspects aside. It shows what each planet signifies, whom it sits with, the life theme each karaka heads, and the Jupiter/Saturn/Rahu transits that time events.
a.featBirthChart: Your chart and everything read directly from it, in tabs: the chart itself, your ascendant and birth star, the yogas and doshas that were found, and the day's panchanga for your birthplace. In Everything mode two more tabs appear: Aspects (which planets "look at" which houses) and Advanced, where you can draw any divisional chart, from D2 up to D60.
a.featChakras: Traditional diagrams — Sarvatobhadra, Kota, Kaala and Tripataki — that arrange stars and signs into grids and wheels to judge transits. Visual, old, and for the curious.
a.featCompare: Put two charts side by side and see how they differ. Unlike Compatibility this is not match-making — it is a neutral comparison, useful for family members or for understanding two people you know.
a.featCompatibility: Traditional match-making between two charts. Guna Milan scores the Ashtakoot (the classic 36-point match), Dashakoota (the ten-factor South Indian porutham system) and the Mangal-dosha question. The Mangal tab calls a chart Manglik when Mars sits in the 1st, 2nd, 4th, 7th, 8th or 12th house from the Lagna and no classical cancellation applies (Mars in its own or exalted sign, a sign-specific exception, or Jupiter with Mars). That's about 3 charts in 10. The same houses counted from the Moon and Venus are shown as supporting detail. The Birth Chart's Yogas & Doshas tab uses the same rule, so the two always agree. Two more tabs look past the score: 7th House sets out each person's house of partnership, its lord, the marriage significators (Venus and Jupiter) and the Upapada, and Timeline shows how the two people's dasha periods overlap, along with Saturn's pressure on each.
a.featDasha: Vedic astrology's timing system. Your life is divided into planetary periods that run for years, each with sub-periods inside it, so a chart's promises are tied to *when*. If you only learn one advanced idea, make it this one. Vimsottari is shown by default; the picker also has the other nakshatra systems (Yogini, Ashtottari and more), the sign-based dashas of the Jaimini school (Narayana, Chara, Sthira and others), Kalachakra, and Sudarshana Chakra, which reads the same period from the Lagna, Moon and Sun at once.
a.featEphemeris: A plain table of where the planets are on any given day — the raw astronomical data behind everything else.
a.featFortnightly: The same idea as Today, widened to the next two weeks — for planning rather than checking in.
a.featGochara: The classical texts' stated results for each planet transiting each house from your Moon — including vedha, the rule where one transit cancels another's effect.
a.featJaimini: A separate classical school with its own logic: it ranks the planets by degree into karakas (significators) and reads the chart from those. Different vocabulary from the rest of the app, and firmly specialist. The page shows the chara karakas, with the Atmakaraka (the planet of the self) first, then the Karakamsa and Swamsa charts drawn from it, and argala, which houses help or block each other.
a.featJournal: Log real events from your life against the planetary periods that were running. Over time this is how you find out whether any of it tracks for you.
a.featKp: Krishnamurti Paddhati — a twentieth-century school that slices the chart much more finely (sub-lords) and is known for precise yes/no answers. A specialist system; skip it unless you already follow it.
a.featLearn: A quiz on your own chart. The AI asks, you answer, it grades and explains. The fastest way to stop needing this help page.
a.featLifeReport: A long, composed reading of your whole chart in seven chapters — personality, career, wealth, relationships, health, purpose and your current outlook. Generated on our server, so you can close the page and come back to it.
a.featMonthly: Your month ahead in one summary.
a.featMuhurta: Choosing a good moment. Give it a window and a purpose — a wedding, travel, signing something — and it finds the times traditionally considered supportive.
a.featNow: The sky as it is right now, cast as a chart in its own right — its own ascendant, today's panchanga and the running hora — rather than laid over a birth chart the way Transits are. It is cast for the current location you set in Settings → Location, falling back to your birth place, and it always says which of the two it used: the ascendant moves a degree every four minutes, so the wrong place is a different chart, not a rounder one. The page and its dashboard tile appear in Everything mode; you can ask the AI about the moment from any page.
a.featPanchaPakshi: A South Indian timing system that assigns you one of five birds and divides the day into periods where your bird is eating, walking, ruling, sleeping or dying. Unusual and self-contained.
a.featPrashna: Horary astrology: instead of your birth chart, it reads a chart cast for the moment you ask a question. Used when the question matters more than the person.
a.featRectify: For an uncertain birth time. Give it a range and some dated life events, and it suggests which times fit best. Experimental by nature — it narrows possibilities rather than proving one.
a.featRemedies: The traditional remedial suggestions — gemstones, mantras, charity — for the planets that look strained in your chart. Offered as tradition, not prescription.
a.featReport: Everything the app can compute about your chart, laid out as one print-ready document you can save as a PDF or hand to someone.
a.featSadeSati: Saturn's roughly seven-and-a-half-year passage over and around your Moon — the cycle most people have heard of and worry about. This shows when yours run and which phase you are in. It is traditionally read as demanding rather than doomed.
a.featSensitivePoints: Specific calculated points in the chart — the special lagnas and upagrahas, the sphutas, the 36 Sahams, and argala — that experienced readers use for fine detail. Comfortably skippable at first.
a.featStrength: How strong each planet is, by the traditional measures. Shadbala scores each one against the minimum it is meant to reach, and Bhava Bala does the same for the houses. Useful for judging which parts of a chart actually carry weight. Vimsopaka rates each planet across the divisional charts, out of 20. The Composition tab shows what each planet's Shadbala is made of — the six component strengths as bars, with the exact figures in a table beneath.
a.featTimeline: Your planetary periods, Sade Sati, and major planetary movements laid out on one scrollable timeline, so you can see how the phases of your life line up.
a.featTithiPravesha: Another way to cast a year-ahead chart. Instead of the Sun returning to its birth position (that is Varshaphal), it uses the return of your birth lunar day.
a.featToday: A short daily briefing for you specifically — the day's almanac, which planetary period you're in, and what's moving over your chart. The best page to check habitually.
a.featTransit: Where the planets are right now, laid over your birth chart — what the sky is currently doing to your map, with an AI reading of it.
a.featVarshaphal: Your year ahead, from a chart cast for the moment the Sun returns to its exact birth position. A separate classical system (Tajaka) with its own year-lord and periods. It shows the Muntha (the point that moves one sign a year and colours that year), the year-lord, the Tajaka Sahams and the annual dasha.
a.featVedicClock: The day as traditional time-keeping sees it, plus which planets are currently retrograde.
a.noBirthTime: Yes. Two options. You can set the time accuracy to "unknown" when you save the profile — the app then reads your chart from the Moon instead of the ascendant, and quietly avoids the things that need an exact time. Or, if you know roughly when you were born and can remember a few dated life events, Birth Time Rectification will suggest the times that best fit them. Treat its answer as a good guess, not a fact.
a.northVsSouth: There are two common ways to draw the same chart. In the North Indian style the houses stay in fixed positions and the signs move; in the South Indian style the signs stay fixed and the houses move. The planets are identical either way — it's the same information in a different frame. Pick whichever you grew up with in Settings → General. In the same place, Sign labels chooses how each house names its sign: a number, a glyph, both, or a short name.
a.privDelete: Settings → Account → Delete account. It removes the account and cascades through everything attached to it: profiles, charts, readings, chats, journal entries, shared links and settings. It's immediate and can't be undone.
a.privEmails: Only what you switch on — the daily or periodic digest, and password resets. Digests are off until you enable them, and every one has an unsubscribe link. You can add other recipients, but only after they confirm.
a.privKeys: Only if you want to use a cloud AI provider under your own account. A key is a password that lets this app use your allowance at, say, OpenAI or Google. Stored encrypted, and shown to you only masked. If you use a local model instead, you never need one.
a.privSharing: You get a link that shows a read-only copy of that chart to anyone who opens it — no login needed. Treat it as public: a link is a key, so only send it to people you'd show the birth details to. You can revoke it later.
a.privWhatStored: Your account (username, email, name), the birth profiles you create, the charts and readings you generate, your settings, and your journal entries if you write any. It lives in this app's own database. It isn't sold, shared or mined. The free preview on the front page stores nothing at all — its details stay in your browser tab until you sign up.
a.rasiVsNavamsa: The Rasi (also called D1) is your main birth chart — the actual sky. The Navamsa (D9) is a derived chart that magnifies one part of the picture: it's traditionally read for marriage, partnership and inner strength, and as a second opinion on how well a planet really does. A planet that looks weak in the Rasi but strong in the Navamsa is the classic "grows into it" signature.
a.retrograde: Planets sometimes appear to move backwards from where we stand, because we're orbiting too. Nothing physically reverses. Astrologically a retrograde planet is usually read as turned inward or revisiting something rather than as bad news.
a.whatAmILookingAt: A map of the sky, flattened. The twelve compartments are the houses — twelve areas of life, in a fixed order starting from your ascendant. The abbreviations inside them are planets. So "Sun in the 10th" means the Sun sat in the part of the sky your tradition associates with career and public standing. That's the whole grammar: a planet, in a sign, in a house.
a.whatIsChart: A snapshot of the sky at the moment you were born, drawn as a diagram. Astrology treats that snapshot as a map of your life's themes. The map has twelve segments ("houses"), and the position of the Sun, Moon and planets across them is what everything else is read from. You don't need to understand the diagram to use this app — every page explains what it found in words.
a.whatIsHouse: One of twelve areas of life. Roughly: 1st you and your body, 2nd money and family, 3rd effort and siblings, 4th home and mother, 5th children and creativity, 6th work, health and obstacles, 7th partnership, 8th upheaval and inheritance, 9th belief and fortune, 10th career, 11th gains and networks, 12th loss, retreat and release. A planet in a house colours that area.
a.whatIsNakshatra: A finer division of the sky than a sign: 27 of them, each about 13°20' wide, sometimes called lunar mansions. Your "birth star" is the nakshatra the Moon was in when you were born, and it's used for personality detail and — importantly — for the timing system below.
a.whatIsSign: The zodiac is a circle split into twelve 30° signs, and at any moment each planet sits in one of them. The sign describes the *manner* of a planet — Mars in a cautious sign behaves differently from Mars in a bold one. Note that Vedic astrology uses the sidereal zodiac, measured against the actual stars, so your Sun sign here is often one back from the one in a newspaper horoscope. That's expected, not a bug.
a.whatIsThis: It takes your birth date, time and place, works out where the planets were at that moment, and helps you read what Vedic astrology (Jyotish) traditionally makes of it — with an AI that can explain any of it in plain English.
a.whereToStart: Open “Start here” — it explains your Rising sign, Moon sign, birth star and the chapter of life you're in now, in plain words, and offers a few good first questions for the AI astrologer. From there the Birth Chart shows the full picture, and Today tells you what's happening right now.
a.dashboardLayout: In the order a reading actually goes, with related pages grouped together. Start here opens with “Start here” — your chart in plain words — then My Chart, the AI astrologer and Your Periods. Read the chart holds the other classical schools and the written-up Reports. Timing is Dasha & Timeline first, then the Transits running over them. Calendar & muhurta is Sky & Panchanga — the sky's own clock — and Muhurta for picking a moment to act. Then Relationships, and Remedies & practice, where My Notebook keeps your own record. Where several pages are one idea they share a single tile, and once you're on any of them a strip under the page title lists the others, so moving between them is one tap. The menu uses the same sections and groups. If you know what you want, just start typing on the dashboard — the search finds every individual page by name, not just the groups.
a.whereIsPage: Nowhere — every page is still there, at the same address, but pages that belong to one idea now share one entry in the menu and on the dashboard. My Chart: Birth Chart, Bhava Chart, Nakshatra Profile, Planetary Strength, Chart Deep-Dive and Sensitive Points. Your Periods: Today, This Fortnight, This Month, Varshaphal and Tithi Pravesha. Other Systems: Jaimini, KP System, Nadi Karakas, Bhrigu Markers and the Chakras. Reports: Life Report, Full Report and Topic Reading. Dasha & Timeline: Dasha Periods and Life Timeline. Transits: Transits, Gochara-phala, Sade Sati and the Ephemeris. Sky & Panchanga: Almanac, Vedic Clock, Pancha Pakshi and Chart of the Moment. Relationships: Compatibility and Compare Charts. My Notebook: AI History and Astro-Journal. Open the group, then use the strip under the page title — or simply type the page's name into the dashboard search. In Essentials mode the strip shows only the pages Essentials advertises; switch to Everything in Settings to see them all. Bookmarks and links in old readings and emails still open the same page.
a.whyBirthTime: Because the sky changes fast. The "ascendant" — the sign coming up over the horizon — moves to a new sign roughly every two hours, and it decides how the whole chart is laid out. A few minutes usually doesn't matter; a few hours changes almost everything. Date and place matter too, but time is the sensitive one.
a.yogaAndDosha: A yoga is a specific planetary combination said to produce a particular result — many are simply favourable patterns worth knowing about. A dosha is an affliction or rough patch in the chart. Both get named dramatically in traditional texts. Read them as emphasis rather than fate: a chart with a dosha is extremely common, and it isn't a diagnosis. On the Birth Chart's Yogas & Doshas tab you'll see them split into the classical yogas, raja yogas (combinations for rank and success, shown with how strongly they're formed) and doshas such as Mangal or Kaal Sarpa, each marked present or absent. A present dosha also says how common it is, measured on 5,000 sample charts under the app's own rules. Pitru Dosha (the father and ancestors) uses a narrower rule than the underlying engine: the Sun or Rahu in the 9th house, or the Sun in the same sign as Rahu or Ketu. The engine's broader version flagged almost 9 charts in 10, so it said little about any one chart. Manglik uses the same rule as the Compatibility page's Mangal tab: Mars in the 1st, 2nd, 4th, 7th, 8th or 12th house from the Lagna, with no classical cancellation.
a.whatIsArudha:
Your Lagna is where you actually stand; the Arudha Lagna (AL) is how that position appears to everyone else — your image, your standing, the visible face of your life rather than the felt one. It is a Jaimini idea, and it is computed, not guessed: from the Lagna, to its ruling planet, and the same distance onward again. The Upapada (UL) is the same construction for the twelfth house, and is read for the marriage.

So a planet can be doing one thing to how a season feels and another to how it looks. In Everything view the Transit page counts each transiting planet from the Arudha Lagna and the Upapada alongside the Lagna and the Moon, marks AL and UL on the chart, and lists all twelve arudhas below. Nothing there is a verdict — the classical good/bad tables for transits are counted from the Moon, so the arudha columns tell you where a planet is, and leave what it means to you and to the AI reading.
a.featSpecialPoints: Alternative reference points to your rising sign, plus the “shadow planets”. Three of them do real work: the Hora Lagna is read for money and income, the Ghati Lagna for authority and promotion, and the Bhava Lagna for the body — they are read together as a trio, alongside (never instead of) your normal rising sign. The rest, including Gulika and the solar upagrahas, are shown because a traditional chart lists them; the app does not invent meanings for the ones without a settled rule.
a.whatIsKaalaVela: The daylight is split into eight parts, each ruled by a planet; four of those parts are traditionally treated as shadowed — Kaala, Mrityu, Artha Prahara and Yama Ghantaka. When a suggested time falls inside one, it is flagged rather than removed, because these parts often coincide with Rahu Kalam and Gulika Kalam and excluding them all would rule out most of the day. Treat a flag as “prefer another slot if you have one”, not “do not do it”.
a.personalMuhurta: Because it is scored against your chart as well as the almanac. A panchang knows the day — its nakshatra, tithi, weekday and yoga — and that part is the same for everybody in your city. On top of that, each day here is put through your own birth chart: Tara Bala (the day’s star counted from your birth star), Chandra Bala (where the Moon is transiting from your natal Moon), and how your running Vimsottari Mahadasha and Bhukti lords are transiting from that Moon. Those four verdicts move the rating, so an ordinary Tuesday can be your best day of the fortnight and a famously auspicious one can rate poorly for you. Turn off “Score against my chart” to see the plain almanac underneath.
a.whatIsLagnaShuddhi: It is lagna shuddhi — the sign rising during that particular window, counted from your janma rasi (natal Moon sign) and your janma lagna. It is checked per window and not per day, because the rising sign turns over roughly every two hours: that is the reason a muhurta is a clock time rather than a date. The 8th from either is the classical bar on beginning anything, and shows as “Lagna: avoid”; the 6th and 12th are flagged as caution; a kendra or trikona from both reads as strong. A barred window is still listed, ranked last, so you can see why the obvious midday slot is not the recommendation.
a.conditionalDashas: Vimsottari, the 120-year cycle, is the default and applies to everyone. The classics also describe *conditional* dasha systems, each with its own total length, that are meant to be read only when the chart meets a stated condition — Shashtihayani (60 years) when the Sun is in the rising sign, Chaturaaseeti Sama (84) when the 10th lord sits in the 10th house, Dwisatpathi (112), Ashtottari (108), Dwadasottari (112), Panchottari (105) and Shatabdika (100) on their own tests. The Dasha page checks your chart against those rules and shows the ones that pass as recommended chips; clicking one opens its periods. They are a cross-check on Vimsottari's timing, not a replacement for it — and where two systems disagree, tradition reads the one whose condition your chart actually meets more heavily.
a.aiDigestHistory: Yes. Every digest that is actually delivered — by email or as a browser notification, for each person it covered — is now saved to AI History under the “Digests” filter, and opens back up on its own page exactly as it was sent. Digests are kept separately from your chats and readings, so a daily email can never push your conversations out of your history.
a.aiDidThisLand: Yes. Every saved reading — on the AI History page, and in the "Recent readings" panel on the tool that produced it — carries a "Did this land?" control: mark it as happened, partly, too early to tell, or it didn't, add what actually came about in your own words, and optionally log it to your astro-journal in the same step. Settled verdicts (everything except "too early to tell") are fed back into later readings, so the AI can see which of your chart's indications have already been borne out — and which you told it were wrong.
a.aiTrackRecord: It is the tally of your own verdicts: how many readings you marked as happened, partly, or didn't, and a hit rate over those. "Too early to tell" is deliberately excluded from the rate — a prediction whose window has not closed says nothing about accuracy yet — and a partial hit counts as half. Verdicts outlive the readings they judge, so the tally is not reset when older readings age out of your history.
a.aiYourData: On Ask AI Astrologer, open "Answer mode, context & charts to consult" — under **Context sections** there is a line for your own record, showing how many outcomes and journal entries the AI can currently see for the selected profile. The two reach it differently: your recorded outcomes go up with the chart in **both** answer modes, while journal entries are fetched on demand and so need **Smart lookup** (Full context sends no tools). Neither is a section of your chart, so neither has a toggle row — the line is there so you can see the capability exists. The full list of everything the AI can fetch, including "Did this land?", is on the AI Tools page under **Your data**.
a.digestCautions: Because a reading that only ever reports good news is not a reading. The digest now also carries what the classical texts call difficult for you: an unfavourable gochara (transit measured from your birth Moon), a favourable one cancelled by vedha (another planet obstructing it), Ashtama or Ardhashtama Sani, the Vishti karana, and the periods traditionally kept clear for anything newly begun — Rahu Kalam and its companions. Each one is marked either “today”, meaning it is what is different about this day, or “ongoing”, meaning it is a backdrop you have been living with for weeks or months. None of it is a prediction of misfortune: it is a note about what to handle with care, and the digest always leaves you something you can do.
a.digestTaraBala: Tara Bala is the tradition's own answer to “is today a good day *for me*”. You count from your birth star (the nakshatra the Moon was in when you were born) to the star running today; the count lands on one of nine Taras, each with a name and a verdict — Sampat (gain), Kshema (safety) and Sadhaka (accomplishment) are the strong ones; Vipat, Pratyak and Vadha are the ones to move gently through. It leads the digest because it is the one thing in your reading that genuinely changes every single day: your dasha turns over in months, a Saturn transit in years, but the Moon moves to a new star every day or so. On the fortnight and month pages the same count is applied to every day of the window, so you get the actual dates worth acting on. It sits alongside Chandra Bala, the gochara verdicts and the Sarvatobhadra chakra — four independent measures that sometimes disagree. That is normal, and the reading will tell you so rather than splitting the difference.
a.digestWindowOverlap: Because two different traditions are dividing the same daylight and they do not have to agree. The Choghadiya splits the day into eight parts and names the good ones (Amrit, Shubh, Labh); Rahu Kalam, Yamaganda and Gulika Kalam are a separate eightfold division of the very same hours. Nothing stops an Amrit window from landing squarely inside Yamaganda, and when it does the digest says so — \u201cAmrit 07:36\u201309:09 (overlaps Yamaganda)\u201d \u2014 instead of recommending the hour in one line and forbidding it in the next. Most practitioners treat the collision as weakening the good window, so read it as \u201cthe best hour available today, with a caveat\u201d rather than a clear run. We state the conflict rather than resolving it for you: which division takes precedence is genuinely disputed, and the Muhurta page gives you both so you can judge.
a.digestReadingShape: The reading is written by a new prompt. The old one asked for every signal of the day in one short note, which meant a sentence each and the same shape every morning; the new one leads on whichever signal is genuinely strongest that day, reads your birth chart to say which part of your life it touches (the house your current dasha lord sits in and the houses it rules), varies how it opens from one day to the next, and avoids re-arguing what it told you yesterday. In the email, the reading is no longer followed by the same facts again as bullet lists \u2014 it was written from those \u2014 so what remains under it is a short \u201cAt a glance\u201d of the things a short note cannot carry: clock times, dates and the next ingress. Everything the digest computes is still on the Daily Digest page in full.
a.eventAlerts: Yes. Open Life Timeline and switch to “What's coming”: it lists the dated things ahead of you — when your dasha period changes, when Saturn enters or leaves one of its hard phases, when Jupiter, Saturn or Mars changes sign, when a planet turns retrograde, and when an eclipse lands on one of your own nakshatras. Each is counted from your Lagna and your Moon, so it says which part of life it touches rather than just naming a planet. Turn on “Event alerts” in Settings › Notifications and you will be emailed (or sent a browser notification) as each one arrives — you choose which kinds matter and how many days of warning you want. Unlike the daily digest, which comes because it is morning, an alert comes only because something actually changed, and you are told once per event.
a.offline: Partly, and it says so when it does. Every number in the app is worked out on the server, so a page you have never opened cannot be shown offline. But a page you *have* opened is saved on your device as it loads, and if you open the app on a plane or in a metro it shows you that saved copy with a strip across the top telling you when it was saved. AI readings are not saved this way — they are in your reading history instead, which needs a connection to open. Everything saved for offline use is cleared when you sign out.
a.accessibility: Yes. Every page starts with a “Skip to content” link so you are not walked through the whole menu first, the menu closes with Escape, and the tab bars move with the arrow keys. The chart itself is described out loud rather than announced as a picture — a screen reader reads the ascendant and then each sign or house with what is sitting in it. If you find something that cannot be reached from the keyboard, that is a bug worth reporting.
a.aiCitations: From a small library of out-of-copyright translations kept with the app — at present the 1885 English translation of Varaha Mihira's *Brihat Jataka*, plus a set of plainly-stated general principles. When a reading cites a chapter and verse, that verse is really in the book; the app never invents a reference. The general principles are labelled “General principle” rather than given a false verse number, so you can always tell which is which. The library is deliberately small, so many readings will have nothing to cite — those simply argue from the chart.
a.featNakshatraGochara: On the Transits page, under the main table. A sign is 30 degrees wide and a planet can sit in one for years; a nakshatra is 13°20', so it says far more about timing. This shows which of the 27 stars each planet is currently crossing, the dates it entered and leaves (including when a retrograde planet turns back into the star behind it), and — the part that is about you — the tarabala: that star counted from your own birth star, which gives one of nine classical results from Sampat (gain) to Vadha (avoid anything irreversible). Each star's deity and symbol are shown too, but labelled as imagery: the classical texts give no table of results for 'planet X in star Y', so nothing here pretends one exists.
a.languageAndTheme: Yes. Settings → General → Language switches between English, Hindi and Sanskrit (Sanskrit is still a work in progress). Hindi doesn't cover every screen yet: sign, star and planet names, the main pages and the newcomer screens (Start here, the welcome steps, the checklist) are translated, while some longer explanations, including many Help answers, still appear in English. The front page has its own English / हिन्दी button beside the theme switch, so you can read it in Hindi before signing in. The theme — Light, Dark, or System to follow your device — is in the same place, and the sun/moon button in the page header flips it in one tap. Printed reports always come out light.
a.whatIsVarga: A divisional chart, or varga, splits each sign into smaller slices and rebuilds the chart from them, to magnify one area of life. The Navamsa (D9) is the best known — marriage and inner strength — and the Dasamsa (D10) is read for career. Others cover siblings (D3), children (D7), parents (D12), and so on up to the very fine D60. They're all on the Birth Chart page under the Advanced tab; pick one from the list to draw it.
a.whatIsAyanamsa: Vedic astrology measures the zodiac against the fixed stars, and the stars have slowly drifted from where Western astrology's zodiac starts. The ayanamsa is how big that drift is taken to be, and different schools use slightly different values — which is why two apps can put a planet a degree apart, or even in a different nakshatra. This app defaults to True Chitra (a precise form of Lahiri) with mean Rahu and Ketu, which matches Jagannatha Hora. You can pick another — plain Lahiri, KP, Raman and others — in Settings → General → Ayanamsa.
a.calendarFeed: Yes. Settings → Calendar gives you a subscription link for Google Calendar, Apple Calendar or Outlook, carrying your chart's upcoming events — bhukti changes, Sade Sati boundaries, your solar return, slow-planet ingresses and eclipses on your birth stars. It refreshes by itself about twice a day. Anyone who has the link can see the feed (calendar apps can't log in), so keep it private.
a.apiAccess: Yes, if you're comfortable with a little setup. Settings → API access creates a personal token for the read-only API, and the same token works with the app's MCP server, which lets an AI assistant such as Claude Desktop look up your charts. The token acts as you, so treat it like a password; you can revoke it there at any time. Nothing reached this way can change your data.
a.featPredictions: An AI reading of your chart on just one area of life — your life path, career, relationships, health, wealth, education or travel — instead of everything at once. Pick the topic and the AI reads the houses, lords, yogas and running dasha that bear on it; for career it also checks the 10th house counted from the Ghati Lagna, the classical second opinion on rise in standing. Wealth is checked the same way from the Hora Lagna, and education against the D24, the divisional chart for learning. It sits with the Life Report and Full Report in Reports, and every reading is saved to your AI History. Health readings are astrology, not medical advice.
a.featStart: The best first stop. It explains four things from your chart in everyday words: your Rising sign (Lagna — how you meet the world), your Moon sign (Rashi — your mind and feelings), your birth star (Nakshatra — the Moon's exact star group, with its traditional symbol and deity), and the chapter of life you're in now (your current dasha period and sub-period, with dates). Each card shows the Sanskrit name beside the plain one, so you'll recognise it on other pages. Nothing on it is written by the AI — it's worked out from your chart instantly — and if your birth time isn't known, it says what can't be stated without it instead of guessing. Underneath are a few questions you can send straight to the AI astrologer.

firstLook.intro: Four things from your birth chart that are worth knowing first. Each one has a Sanskrit name — it's shown beside the plain one so you'll recognise it elsewhere in the app.
firstLook.risingWhat: The sign coming up over the eastern horizon at the moment you were born. It describes how you meet the world.
firstLook.moonWhat: The sign the Moon was in. In Vedic astrology it describes your mind and feelings — many people relate to it more than to their Sun sign.
firstLook.starWhat: The Moon's position narrowed to one of 27 star groups, each about 13° wide. It's the most personal of the three.
firstLook.starLine: Its symbol is the {{symbol}} and its deity {{deity}}. Traditionally linked with: {{theme}}.
firstLook.chapterWhat: Vedic astrology divides a life into long periods, each ruled by one planet. They're how it talks about timing.

rising.1: You meet life head-on: quick to start, direct, and at your best when there's something to go after.
rising.2: You come across as steady and grounded — patient, loyal, and drawn to comfort, beauty and things that last.
rising.3: You meet the world with curiosity: talkative, quick-witted, and happiest when there's something new to learn.
rising.4: You lead with feeling: protective, caring, and deeply tied to home, family and the people you call yours.
rising.5: You come across with warmth and presence — generous, proud, and naturally drawn to lead or to shine.
rising.6: You meet life with a careful eye: practical, helpful, and good at noticing what others miss.
rising.7: You come across as gracious and fair — a natural diplomat who looks for balance and partnership.
rising.8: You meet the world with intensity: private, perceptive, slow to trust and deeply loyal once you do.
rising.9: You come across as open and hopeful — a seeker who wants meaning, freedom and the bigger picture.
rising.10: You meet life with patience and ambition: responsible, disciplined, and built for the long climb.
rising.11: You come across as independent and original — drawn to ideas, to groups, and to doing things your own way.
rising.12: You meet the world softly: imaginative, compassionate, and sensitive to what others feel.

moon.1: Emotionally you are quick and fiery — you feel things fast, say them plainly, and recover just as fast.
moon.2: Emotionally you need security and calm: steady routines, good food, and people you can rely on.
moon.3: Emotionally you need variety and conversation — talking things through is how you make sense of them.
moon.4: Emotionally you are tender and protective; home and family are where you recharge.
moon.5: Emotionally you need to be appreciated — warmth, loyalty and a little recognition keep you bright.
moon.6: Emotionally you settle by sorting things out — being useful and having things in order calms you.
moon.7: Emotionally you need harmony and good company; conflict unsettles you more than most.
moon.8: Emotionally you feel deeply and privately — intense, loyal, and slow to let go.
moon.9: Emotionally you need freedom and something to look forward to; optimism is your natural setting.
moon.10: Emotionally you are reserved and self-reliant — you feel safest when things are under control.
moon.11: Emotionally you need space and friendship; you would rather understand a feeling than be swept away by it.
moon.12: Emotionally you are sensitive and intuitive, absorbing the moods around you — quiet time restores you.

ai.title: Answers you can trace back.
ai.intro: Most astrology apps hand you a confident paragraph and hope you believe it. {{site}} shows its work.
points: Every reading is grounded in your actual computed positions — not a generic sun-sign.
Claims are cited to the classical texts they draw from, so you can read the source yourself.
When the tradition is silent, it says so instead of inventing a verdict.
One tap toggles between plain language and full technical depth.

demo.q: When does my career finally settle down?
demo.a: Your tenth house is ruled by Saturn, which turns strong in its own sign during the Saturn–Mercury period beginning late 2027. Classical timing links this pairing to steady, earned advancement rather than sudden change¹. Transit Jupiter reinforces it by crossing your tenth in the same window².
